Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Event Recall: Talking about the event, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Avoid People: avoid other people, Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Vignette:
Six years ago, Marcus Thorne was driving Route 14 through a heavy downpour when a passenger aboard lost control, swinging a metal water bottle at a sleeping commuter. Marcus had to break a two-armed hold around his neck to intervene, pressing the man to the floor until his breathing slowed. The police arrived three minutes later, sirens cutting through the rain, and in the confusion, the officers tackled Marcus anyway, assuming he was the aggressor. He spent four hours in a holding cell before they reviewed the dashcam footage and released him. What frightened him most was how quickly his own efforts had been read as a threat, how the uniforms that were supposed to bring safety had instead confirmed his suspicion that the world is a dangerous place. Over the following months, he developed a rhythm of checking the apartment door and windows, turning each deadbolt and latch multiple times until the metal clicked into place. He felt untethered from the cultural gatherings and familiar faces of his neighborhood, a hollowed-out sense of disconnection that simply was. When colleagues asked what had happened, he would find himself speaking about the incident and quickly stop, realizing how easily the words had slipped out. Marcus returned to driving, but the first time a marked cruiser fell in behind his bus, a memory of the event came to mind suddenly, absolute and unbidden. He brought both hands up to cover his face, hiding behind them until the cruiser pulled away. He began avoiding other people on his route, leaning forward over the steering wheel, keeping his eyes fixed on the road and refusing to meet the gaze of anyone who boarded. On his lunch breaks, he sat in the depot bathroom with the radio turned so loud it rattled the metal stall doors, using the volume to occupy his senses. Irritability settled into his days, surfacing as sharp outbursts when a passenger questioned his routing or a supervisor asked about his missed stops; his concentration slipped during long stretches, and his hands kept drifting to his face whenever any authority figure appeared. He was certain that no one would believe him if he explained his side of things; people could not be trusted to see what had actually happened. The habits hardened over weeks and months. At home, the television became his constant companion, filling the apartment so he would not have to sit with the silence. He stopped returning calls from his sister, keeping his distance while the anger that sometimes leaked out of him without warning remained. At work, he requested temporary transfers away from routes near police stations, but the depot manager noted his declining attendance and the growing tension with his fellow drivers. What finally brought Marcus to the clinic was a morning when he realized he could no longer complete his run without feeling his pulse spike at the sight of any marked vehicle, and he feared he would lose his license altogether. He hopes to find a way to sit in his bus again without covering his face or waiting for the loud music to save him, though he worries that seeking help might only mean being asked to talk about the event until he has to do it all over again.
